C is wrong: Instance Connect removes long-lived keys but still needs port 22 open, and it does not record the commands run in a session.
D is wrong: a NAT gateway only lets instances start outbound connections, so it gives administrators no way in at all.
tldr: Session Manager needs no inbound ports or SSH keys, and it logs every session's commands for audit.

wrong_reasons.B: it still depends on inbound SSH and on distributing and rotating SSH keys, and it records nothing about what is typed in each session.
wrong_reasons.C: Instance Connect removes long-lived keys but still needs port 22 open, and it does not record the commands run in a session.
wrong_reasons.D: a NAT gateway only lets instances start outbound connections, so it gives administrators no way in at all.

question: A company runs an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance that was created without encryption. A new compliance requirement states that the database and its automated backups must be encrypted at rest with a customer managed AWS KMS key. Some downtime during a maintenance window is acceptable. What should a solutions architect do?
hint: Encryption is a creation-time choice for an RDS instance. Which artifact can you encrypt on the way through?
keywords: Some downtime during a maintenance window is acceptable

options.A: Modify the DB instance to enable encryption with the customer managed key, and apply the change during the next maintenance window.
options.B: Take a snapshot of the DB instance, copy the snapshot with encryption enabled using the customer managed key, restore a new DB instance from the encrypted copy, and point the application at the new instance.
options.C: Create an encrypted read replica of the unencrypted DB instance with the customer managed key, then promote the replica to a standalone DB instance.
options.D: Turn on EBS encryption by default in the account and reboot the DB instance so that its storage is re-encrypted.

explanation: A is wrong: RDS does not let you turn on encryption for an existing unencrypted DB instance by modifying it.

B is correct: encryption can only be chosen when an RDS DB instance is created, but copying an unencrypted snapshot lets you encrypt the copy with a KMS key, and a DB instance restored from it is encrypted together with all of its future automated backups and snapshots.
C is wrong: RDS does not allow an encrypted read replica of an unencrypted DB instance, which is exactly why this shortcut is tempting and unavailable.
D is wrong: the account-level EBS encryption default applies to new EC2 volumes and has no effect on the storage of an existing RDS DB instance.
tldr: Encryption can only be set at RDS instance creation -- encrypt via a snapshot copy and restore to change it after the fact.

wrong_reasons.A: RDS does not let you turn on encryption for an existing unencrypted DB instance by modifying it.
wrong_reasons.C: RDS does not allow an encrypted read replica of an unencrypted DB instance, which is exactly why this shortcut is tempting and unavailable.
wrong_reasons.D: the account-level EBS encryption default applies to new EC2 volumes and has no effect on the storage of an existing RDS DB instance.

question: An application on Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets reads and writes objects in an Amazon S3 bucket through an S3 gateway VPC endpoint. The security team requires that the bucket reject every request that does not arrive through that specific endpoint, and every request that is not sent over TLS, even if the caller's IAM policy allows the action. Which combination of bucket policy statements meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)
hint: Only an explicit Deny beats an Allow the caller already has. Which condition keys identify the endpoint and the transport?
keywords: reject every request that does not arrive through that specific endpoint
even if the caller's IAM policy allows the action

options.A: A Deny statement for all principals and all S3 actions with a StringNotEquals condition on aws:SourceVpce set to the gateway endpoint's ID.
options.B: A Deny statement for all principals and all S3 actions with a Bool condition on aws:SecureTransport set to false.
options.C: A Deny statement for all principals and all S3 actions with a NotIpAddress condition on aws:SourceIp set to the private subnets' CIDR ranges.
options.D: An Allow statement that grants all S3 actions to the instance role only when aws:SecureTransport is true.
options.E: A Deny statement for s3:PutObject requests that do not include the x-amz-server-side-encryption header.

explanation: A is correct: requests through a gateway endpoint carry the endpoint ID in aws:SourceVpce, so an explicit Deny whenever it does not match blocks every other path to the bucket, and an explicit Deny overrides any Allow in the caller's IAM policy.
B is correct: aws:SecureTransport is false for requests made over plain HTTP, so an explicit Deny on that condition rejects anything not sent over TLS.
C is wrong: aws:SourceIp does not carry the private address of a request that arrives through a VPC endpoint, so this Deny would block the application's own traffic.
D is wrong: an Allow cannot take away an Allow the caller already has in an IAM policy in the same account, so plain-HTTP requests would still succeed; only an explicit Deny enforces the rule.
E is wrong: that header controls encryption at rest for new objects, not whether a request used TLS or came through the endpoint.
tldr: Deny policies keyed on aws:SourceVpce and aws:SecureTransport together lock S3 access to one VPC endpoint over TLS only.

wrong_reasons.C: aws:SourceIp does not carry the private address of a request that arrives through a VPC endpoint, so this Deny would block the application's own traffic.
wrong_reasons.D: an Allow cannot take away an Allow the caller already has in an IAM policy in the same account, so plain-HTTP requests would still succeed; only an explicit Deny enforces the rule.
wrong_reasons.E: that header controls encryption at rest for new objects, not whether a request used TLS or came through the endpoint.

question: Workloads in several VPCs send outbound traffic to the internet through a central egress VPC with NAT gateways, connected by AWS Transit Gateway. The security team now requires that outbound HTTPS be allowed only to an approved list of domain names, such as the operating system vendor's update servers and a payment provider, and that all other outbound traffic be blocked and logged. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
hint: Security groups and network ACLs only understand IP addresses. What can inspect the domain name in outbound HTTPS?

options.A: Deploy AWS Network Firewall in the egress VPC, route traffic from the transit gateway through the firewall endpoints before the NAT gateways, and use a stateful domain list rule group that allows only the approved domains.
options.B: Add outbound rules to every workload security group that allow HTTPS only to the approved domain names.
options.C: Add network ACL rules in the egress VPC that allow HTTPS only to the IP addresses the approved domains resolve to today.
options.D: Run a fleet of self-managed proxy servers on Amazon EC2 in the egress VPC and maintain the allowlist in their configuration.

explanation: A is correct: Network Firewall is a managed, stateful firewall whose domain list rule groups match the TLS SNI and HTTP Host header against allowed domain names, and placing it in the central egress path enforces and logs the policy for every VPC at once.
B is wrong: security group rules accept IP addresses, CIDR blocks, prefix lists or other security groups, not domain names.
C is wrong: network ACLs also work on IP addresses only, and the addresses behind these domains change over time, so the allowlist would silently drift out of date.
D is wrong: a proxy fleet can filter by domain, but the company would have to patch, scale and keep highly available the infrastructure that Network Firewall provides as a managed service.
tldr: A centralized Network Firewall in the egress path enforces and logs domain-based outbound rules for every VPC at once.

wrong_reasons.B: security group rules accept IP addresses, CIDR blocks, prefix lists or other security groups, not domain names.
wrong_reasons.C: network ACLs also work on IP addresses only, and the addresses behind these domains change over time, so the allowlist would silently drift out of date.
wrong_reasons.D: a proxy fleet can filter by domain, but the company would have to patch, scale and keep highly available the infrastructure that Network Firewall provides as a managed service.

question: A content management system runs on Linux Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group across three Availability Zones. Every instance must read and write the same set of uploaded media files, and the files must remain available if one Availability Zone fails. Which storage option meets these requirements?
hint: Shared by many Linux instances at once, and still there after losing a zone.
keywords: read and write the same set
remain available if one Availability Zone fails

options.A: An Amazon EBS io2 volume with Multi-Attach enabled, attached to every instance.
options.B: An Amazon EFS file system using a Regional storage class, mounted on every instance through a mount target in each Availability Zone.
options.C: An instance store volume on each instance, kept in sync between instances by a cron job.
options.D: An Amazon FSx for Windows File Server file system in a Single-AZ deployment.

explanation: A is wrong: Multi-Attach works only for instances in the same Availability Zone as the volume and needs a cluster-aware file system, so it cannot serve three zones.

B is correct: EFS Regional storage classes store data redundantly across multiple Availability Zones and provide a shared NFS file system that instances in every zone can mount at the same time, so the media survives the loss of a zone.
C is wrong: instance store data is lost when an instance stops or fails, and a cron job leaves the copies inconsistent between runs.
D is wrong: FSx for Windows File Server serves SMB shares for Windows workloads, and a Single-AZ deployment does not survive the loss of its Availability Zone.
tldr: EFS gives a shared, Multi-AZ NFS file system that every instance in an Auto Scaling group can mount concurrently.

wrong_reasons.A: Multi-Attach works only for instances in the same Availability Zone as the volume and needs a cluster-aware file system, so it cannot serve three zones.
wrong_reasons.C: instance store data is lost when an instance stops or fails, and a cron job leaves the copies inconsistent between runs.
wrong_reasons.D: FSx for Windows File Server serves SMB shares for Windows workloads, and a Single-AZ deployment does not survive the loss of its Availability Zone.

question: During flash sales, an order service on Amazon EC2 writes each order directly to an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL database. Write bursts exceed what the database can absorb, requests time out, and some orders are lost. Outside sales the load is modest, and the business accepts that orders are confirmed to customers a few seconds after they are placed. Which change prevents lost orders MOST cost-effectively?
hint: Customers can wait a few seconds for confirmation. What can hold the burst while the database catches up?
keywords: Write bursts exceed what the database can absorb
a few seconds after they are placed

options.A: Have the order service send each order to an Amazon SQS queue, and have a group of workers consume the queue and write to the database at a rate it can sustain.
options.B: Scale the database up permanently to the largest instance class so that it can absorb the peak.
options.C: Add RDS read replicas and spread the order writes across them.
options.D: Put an Amazon ElastiCache cluster in front of the database to hold the orders.

explanation: A is correct: the queue durably stores every order during a burst and lets the workers drain it at the database's pace, which decouples the write rate from the arrival rate and stops orders being lost without paying for peak database capacity.
B is wrong: paying for peak capacity all year to cover a few hours of sales is the costly option, and a larger burst can still overwhelm it.
C is wrong: read replicas are read-only, so they cannot accept the order writes.
D is wrong: a cache speeds up repeated reads but is not a durable buffer for writes, so orders held in it can still be lost.
tldr: A queue between app and database decouples burst write rate from the database's absorb rate, so nothing is lost or timed out.

wrong_reasons.B: paying for peak capacity all year to cover a few hours of sales is the costly option, and a larger burst can still overwhelm it.
wrong_reasons.C: read replicas are read-only, so they cannot accept the order writes.
wrong_reasons.D: a cache speeds up repeated reads but is not a durable buffer for writes, so orders held in it can still be lost.

question: A global social app stores user profiles in an Amazon DynamoDB table in us-east-1. Users in Europe and Asia see high write latency, and the business now requires that the app keep accepting reads and writes in the remaining Regions if an entire AWS Region becomes unavailable, with each Region serving its local users. Which solution meets these requirements?
hint: Every Region must take writes on its own. Which DynamoDB feature makes each replica writable?
keywords: keep accepting reads and writes in the remaining Regions
each Region serving its local users

options.A: Convert the table to a DynamoDB global table with replicas in us-east-1, eu-west-1 and ap-southeast-1, and have the app in each Region read and write its local replica.
options.B: Enable DynamoDB point-in-time recovery and restore the table into another Region if us-east-1 fails.
options.C: Add a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster in eu-west-1 and in ap-southeast-1 in front of the us-east-1 table.
options.D: Use DynamoDB Streams and an AWS Lambda function to copy every change into read-only tables in the other two Regions.

explanation: A is correct: a global table keeps a replica in each chosen Region, every replica accepts reads and writes locally, and changes replicate asynchronously between Regions, so users write with local latency and the remaining Regions keep serving if one Region fails.
B is wrong: a restore takes time and loses writes made after the restore point, and it does nothing for everyday write latency.
C is wrong: a DAX cluster must run in the same Region as its table and only caches reads, so writes would still go to us-east-1 and fail with it.
D is wrong: this rebuilds replication by hand, and read-only copies cannot accept writes while us-east-1 is unavailable.
tldr: DynamoDB global tables replicate to every Region with local read/write latency and automatic multi-Region resilience.

wrong_reasons.B: a restore takes time and loses writes made after the restore point, and it does nothing for everyday write latency.
wrong_reasons.C: a DAX cluster must run in the same Region as its table and only caches reads, so writes would still go to us-east-1 and fail with it.
wrong_reasons.D: this rebuilds replication by hand, and read-only copies cannot accept writes while us-east-1 is unavailable.

question: A web application keeps user session data in memory on each Amazon EC2 instance behind an Application Load Balancer. When the Auto Scaling group scales in or an instance fails, the affected users are logged out and lose their shopping carts. Sticky sessions are enabled. Which change makes sessions survive the loss of an instance while keeping the fleet elastic?
hint: Stickiness keeps a user on one instance; it does not keep the data when that instance goes away.
keywords: in memory on each Amazon EC2 instance
scales in or an instance fails

options.A: Increase the sticky session duration so that users stay on one instance for longer.
options.B: Move the session data to an Amazon DynamoDB table keyed by session ID, use Time to Live (TTL) to remove expired sessions, and make the web instances stateless.
options.C: Disable scale-in on the Auto Scaling group so that instances holding sessions are never terminated.
options.D: Store session data on an EBS volume attached to each instance and take snapshots of the volumes every hour.

explanation: A is wrong: stickiness only routes a user back to the same instance, so the session is still lost whenever that instance is terminated or fails, and longer stickiness spreads load less evenly.

B is correct: an external session store keeps session data independent of any single instance, so the load balancer can send a user to any instance and the Auto Scaling group can add or remove instances freely, while TTL clears out old sessions at no extra cost.
C is wrong: it gives up elasticity and its cost savings and still loses sessions when an instance fails.
D is wrong: the data is still tied to one instance, other instances cannot read it, and hourly snapshots lose up to an hour of carts.
tldr: Externalizing session state (with TTL) frees instances to scale freely without users losing their session.

wrong_reasons.A: stickiness only routes a user back to the same instance, so the session is still lost whenever that instance is terminated or fails, and longer stickiness spreads load less evenly.
wrong_reasons.C: it gives up elasticity and its cost savings and still loses sessions when an instance fails.
wrong_reasons.D: the data is still tied to one instance, other instances cannot read it, and hourly snapshots lose up to an hour of carts.

question: An internal reporting application runs on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group with a target tracking policy on CPU utilization. Every weekday, traffic rises from almost nothing to its daily peak between 08:45 and 09:00. New instances take about 10 minutes to boot and load their data caches, so users see slow responses every morning until the group catches up. Which combination of changes will BEST remove the morning slowdown? (Select TWO.)
hint: Two separate delays: noticing the ramp too late, and each new instance taking 10 minutes to become useful.
keywords: about 10 minutes to boot and load their data caches

options.A: Add a predictive scaling policy so that the group launches capacity ahead of the forecast daily ramp.
options.B: Configure a warm pool of pre-initialized instances so that scale-out skips the long boot and cache-loading step.
options.C: Lower the target tracking CPU target from 50% to 20%.
options.D: Change the group's health check type from EC2 to ELB.
options.E: Replace the target tracking policy with a step scaling policy that adds more instances per alarm breach.

explanation: A is correct: predictive scaling learns the recurring weekday pattern from CloudWatch history and launches instances before the ramp begins, instead of reacting after CPU has already risen.

B is correct: a warm pool holds instances that have already booted and loaded their caches in a stopped or running state, so when the group scales out they enter service far faster than a 10-minute cold start.
C is wrong: a lower target keeps more idle capacity all day and still reacts only after the traffic arrives, so the 10-minute warm-up still hits users.
D is wrong: ELB health checks decide when to replace unhealthy instances, not when to add capacity.
E is wrong: bigger steps still start only after the alarm fires, so every new instance still needs its 10-minute warm-up while users wait.
tldr: Predictive scaling pre-launches for a known daily pattern, and a warm pool skips the cold-start wait entirely.

wrong_reasons.C: a lower target keeps more idle capacity all day and still reacts only after the traffic arrives, so the 10-minute warm-up still hits users.
wrong_reasons.D: ELB health checks decide when to replace unhealthy instances, not when to add capacity.
wrong_reasons.E: bigger steps still start only after the alarm fires, so every new instance still needs its 10-minute warm-up while users wait.

question: A company keeps 60 TB of research data on an on-premises NFS file server and adds about 200 GB of new and changed files every day. It wants to copy the existing data to Amazon EFS over its 10 Gbps AWS Direct Connect connection, then keep EFS in sync with the daily changes until cutover in three months, with scheduling, encryption in transit and data integrity checks built in. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational effort?
hint: An ongoing, scheduled, online copy from NFS into an AWS file system. Which managed service is built for exactly that?
keywords: 200 GB of new and changed files every day

options.A: Order AWS Snowball Edge devices for the initial copy, and ship a new device each week for the changes.
options.B: Deploy an AWS DataSync agent on premises, create a task from the NFS share to the EFS file system, and schedule it to run daily.
options.C: Mount the EFS file system on an on-premises server over Direct Connect and run rsync from a cron job.
options.D: Deploy Amazon S3 File Gateway, copy the files into its share, and use AWS Lambda to move them from Amazon S3 into EFS.

explanation: A is wrong: 60 TB crosses a 10 Gbps link in roughly half a day at full line rate, so shipping devices adds days of transit for no benefit, and weekly shipments cannot keep up with daily changes.

B is correct: DataSync transfers only new and changed files on each scheduled run, encrypts data in transit, verifies integrity, and parallelizes transfers to use the available bandwidth, all as a managed service.
C is wrong: rsync copies with limited parallelism, and the company would have to build its own scheduling, retries, monitoring and verification around it.
D is wrong: it adds two services and custom code to reach a destination that DataSync writes to directly.
tldr: DataSync automates incremental, verified, bandwidth-efficient transfer of only new or changed files on a schedule.

wrong_reasons.A: 60 TB crosses a 10 Gbps link in roughly half a day at full line rate, so shipping devices adds days of transit for no benefit, and weekly shipments cannot keep up with daily changes.
wrong_reasons.C: rsync copies with limited parallelism, and the company would have to build its own scheduling, retries, monitoring and verification around it.
wrong_reasons.D: it adds two services and custom code to reach a destination that DataSync writes to directly.

question: A retailer's analysts run complex SQL with multi-table joins and aggregations over 30 TB of recent sales data, and 200 business users open dashboards that must return in a few seconds throughout the day. The analysts also need to join that data occasionally with 400 TB of older, rarely queried history kept in Amazon S3 as Parquet, without loading that history into the warehouse. Which solution BEST meets these requirements?
hint: Warehouse-grade joins for the hot data, and a way to reach the S3 history without loading it.
keywords: without loading that history into the warehouse

options.A: Store the 30 TB in Amazon Redshift, enable concurrency scaling for the dashboard peaks, and query the history in S3 through Redshift Spectrum external tables.
options.B: Load all 430 TB into Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL and add read replicas for the dashboards.
options.C: Query all of the data directly in S3 with Amazon Athena and point the dashboards at Athena.
options.D: Store the data in Amazon DynamoDB and use DynamoDB Streams to precompute the dashboard results.

explanation: A is correct: Redshift is a columnar, massively parallel data warehouse built for complex joins and aggregations, concurrency scaling adds capacity automatically when many dashboard queries arrive at once, and Spectrum queries the Parquet history in place in S3 and joins it with warehouse tables.
B is wrong: a row-oriented transactional database is not built for analytic scans and joins across hundreds of terabytes, and 430 TB exceeds the maximum storage of an RDS DB instance.
C is wrong: Athena suits ad hoc queries, but 200 users running complex dashboards all day run into account-level limits on concurrent queries, and every refresh pays for another scan.
D is wrong: DynamoDB is a key-value store that cannot run SQL joins or ad hoc aggregations, so every analytic question would need custom precomputation.
tldr: Redshift's MPP engine handles heavy joins, concurrency scaling absorbs dashboard spikes, and Spectrum queries S3 data in place.

wrong_reasons.B: a row-oriented transactional database is not built for analytic scans and joins across hundreds of terabytes, and 430 TB exceeds the maximum storage of an RDS DB instance.
wrong_reasons.C: Athena suits ad hoc queries, but 200 users running complex dashboards all day run into account-level limits on concurrent queries, and every refresh pays for another scan.
wrong_reasons.D: DynamoDB is a key-value store that cannot run SQL joins or ad hoc aggregations, so every analytic question would need custom precomputation.

question: A data platform writes hundreds of millions of small objects per day to an Amazon S3 bucket that uses SSE-KMS with a customer managed key. The AWS KMS charges on the bill now exceed the S3 storage cost, and the security team requires that SSE-KMS with the same key remain in use. Which change reduces the KMS cost the MOST?
hint: Keep the key, cut the calls. Which S3 setting stops S3 calling KMS for every single object?
keywords: hundreds of millions of small objects per day
SSE-KMS with a customer managed key

options.A: Enable S3 Bucket Keys for the bucket's SSE-KMS encryption.
options.B: Change the bucket's default encryption to SSE-S3.
options.C: Replace the customer managed key with the AWS managed key for S3 (aws/s3).
options.D: Create a separate customer managed key for each day's data so that requests are spread across more keys.

explanation: A is correct: an S3 Bucket Key is a short-lived, bucket-level key derived from the KMS key that S3 uses to generate data keys itself, so S3 makes far fewer requests to KMS, cutting request costs by up to 99% while the same customer managed key still protects the data.
B is wrong: SSE-S3 removes the KMS charges but breaks the requirement to keep SSE-KMS with the same key.
C is wrong: it replaces the customer managed key the security team requires, and S3 would still call KMS for every object.
D is wrong: every extra key adds a monthly charge and S3 still calls KMS once per object, so this raises the cost instead of lowering it.
tldr: An S3 Bucket Key drastically cuts KMS request costs by reusing a short-lived derived key instead of calling KMS per object.

wrong_reasons.B: SSE-S3 removes the KMS charges but breaks the requirement to keep SSE-KMS with the same key.
wrong_reasons.C: it replaces the customer managed key the security team requires, and S3 would still call KMS for every object.
wrong_reasons.D: every extra key adds a monthly charge and S3 still calls KMS once per object, so this raises the cost instead of lowering it.

question: A company is migrating a Windows Server application with Microsoft SQL Server to Amazon EC2. It already owns SQL Server licenses that are licensed per physical core and are not eligible for License Mobility, so they may be used only on hardware dedicated to the company where it can see the sockets and cores. The company wants to use these existing licenses instead of paying for license-included instances. Which EC2 option meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
hint: Licenses tied to physical cores need hardware where the company can see those cores. Which EC2 option exposes them?

options.A: Launch the instances on Amazon EC2 Dedicated Hosts and use AWS License Manager to track the core-based license usage.
options.B: Launch the instances as Dedicated Instances.
options.C: Launch license-included Windows Server and SQL Server On-Demand Instances and cover them with a Compute Savings Plan.
options.D: Launch Spot Instances and apply the existing licenses to them.

explanation: A is correct: a Dedicated Host is a physical server allocated to the company that exposes its sockets and physical cores, which is what bring-your-own-license terms bound to physical cores require, and License Manager tracks usage against the licenses so the company stays compliant.
B is wrong: Dedicated Instances run on single-tenant hardware but do not expose sockets and cores or give host-level placement control, so they cannot satisfy licenses bound to physical cores.
C is wrong: license-included instances pay again for SQL Server licenses the company already owns, which is exactly the cost it wants to avoid.
D is wrong: Spot Instances run on shared hardware and can be interrupted, so they neither satisfy dedicated-hardware licensing nor suit a production database.
tldr: A Dedicated Host exposes physical sockets/cores for per-core BYOL licensing, tracked for compliance by License Manager.

wrong_reasons.B: Dedicated Instances run on single-tenant hardware but do not expose sockets and cores or give host-level placement control, so they cannot satisfy licenses bound to physical cores.
wrong_reasons.C: license-included instances pay again for SQL Server licenses the company already owns, which is exactly the cost it wants to avoid.
wrong_reasons.D: Spot Instances run on shared hardware and can be interrupted, so they neither satisfy dedicated-hardware licensing nor suit a production database.

question: An application sends about 3 TB of logs per month to Amazon CloudWatch Logs, and its log groups use the default retention setting. Engineers query only the last 30 days, but compliance requires keeping every log for 7 years, with retrieval within 48 hours when an auditor asks. The CloudWatch Logs storage bill grows every month. Which solution is MOST cost-effective?
hint: Keep the recent month where engineers query it, and move the 7-year copy to the cheapest storage that still meets a 48-hour retrieval.

options.A: Set the log groups' retention to 7 years so that older logs expire automatically.
options.B: Set the log groups' retention to 30 days, and add a subscription filter that streams the logs through Amazon Data Firehose to an S3 bucket with a lifecycle rule that transitions objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
options.C: Keep the default retention and create an Amazon OpenSearch Service domain to hold the older logs.
options.D: Set the log groups' retention to 30 days and rely on CloudWatch Logs to archive expired logs to Amazon S3 automatically.

explanation: A is wrong: CloudWatch Logs storage costs far more per GB than S3 Glacier Deep Archive, so keeping 7 years of logs there is the expensive way to meet the requirement.

B is correct: 30-day retention keeps recent logs queryable in CloudWatch, the subscription delivers every event to S3 as it arrives, and Deep Archive is the lowest-cost storage class, with standard retrievals completing within 12 hours, well inside the 48-hour audit window.
C is wrong: the default retention keeps logs in CloudWatch forever, and an OpenSearch domain adds an always-running cluster that costs far more than archival storage.
D is wrong: logs that reach the end of their retention period are deleted, not archived, so everything older than 30 days would be lost.
tldr: Keep recent logs in CloudWatch, ship everything to S3 via subscription, and archive to Deep Archive for cheap long-term retention.

wrong_reasons.A: CloudWatch Logs storage costs far more per GB than S3 Glacier Deep Archive, so keeping 7 years of logs there is the expensive way to meet the requirement.
wrong_reasons.C: the default retention keeps logs in CloudWatch forever, and an OpenSearch domain adds an always-running cluster that costs far more than archival storage.
wrong_reasons.D: logs that reach the end of their retention period are deleted, not archived, so everything older than 30 days would be lost.

question: After a security incident, a company must be able to answer which source IP addresses connected to a particular Amazon EC2 instance, which connections were rejected by security groups or network ACLs, and how many bytes were transferred, for any time in the last 90 days. The instances run a mix of operating systems, and the company does not want to install or maintain agents. What should a solutions architect do?
hint: Which VPC feature records connection metadata, including whether traffic was accepted or rejected, without touching the instances?
keywords: does not want to install or maintain agents

options.A: Enable VPC Flow Logs for the VPC, publish them to an Amazon S3 bucket with a 90-day lifecycle, and query them with Amazon Athena.
options.B: Enable AWS CloudTrail data events for Amazon EC2 in every Region.
options.C: Install the CloudWatch agent on every instance to publish network connection metrics.
options.D: Enable Traffic Mirroring on every elastic network interface and store the packet captures in Amazon S3.

explanation: A is correct: flow logs record accepted and rejected IP traffic at the VPC, subnet or interface level, including source and destination addresses and ports, packet and byte counts and the ACCEPT or REJECT action, with no agent on the instances, and in S3 they can be queried with Athena for as long as the lifecycle keeps them.
B is wrong: CloudTrail records AWS API calls, not the network connections between hosts.
C is wrong: this needs an agent on every instance, which the company rules out, and it cannot show traffic that a security group or network ACL rejected before it reached the instance.
D is wrong: Traffic Mirroring captures whole packets, which costs far more to store than the connection metadata needed here, and it must be configured per interface with mirror targets.
tldr: VPC Flow Logs capture accepted/rejected traffic with no agent, queryable via Athena for incident investigation.

wrong_reasons.B: CloudTrail records AWS API calls, not the network connections between hosts.
wrong_reasons.C: this needs an agent on every instance, which the company rules out, and it cannot show traffic that a security group or network ACL rejected before it reached the instance.
wrong_reasons.D: Traffic Mirroring captures whole packets, which costs far more to store than the connection metadata needed here, and it must be configured per interface with mirror targets.

question: A company is migrating a .NET application to Amazon EC2 Windows instances. The instances must be domain-joined so that employees sign in with their existing corporate Active Directory accounts, and the application relies on integrated Windows authentication. The company wants a managed directory in AWS that trusts its on-premises Active Directory, and it wants minimal ongoing administration. Which solution meets these requirements?
hint: Domain join, Group Policy and Kerberos inside AWS, while the user accounts stay on premises.
keywords: managed directory in AWS that trusts

options.A: Deploy AWS Directory Service for Microsoft Active Directory (AWS Managed Microsoft AD) in the VPC and create a forest trust with the on-premises Active Directory.
options.B: Run a pair of self-managed Active Directory domain controllers on Amazon EC2 and replicate the corporate domain to them.
options.C: Deploy AD Connector and use it as the directory that the instances and application authenticate against.
options.D: Create an Amazon Cognito user pool federated with the corporate directory through SAML.

explanation: A is correct: AWS Managed Microsoft AD is a managed, highly available Microsoft Active Directory running in AWS that supports domain joins, Group Policy and Kerberos-based integrated Windows authentication, and a forest trust lets it accept the company's existing on-premises accounts without duplicating them.
B is wrong: self-managed domain controllers mean patching, backups, monitoring and replication design, which is the ongoing administration the company wants to avoid.

C is wrong: AD Connector is a proxy that redirects requests to the on-premises directory rather than a directory in AWS, so every authentication depends on the on-premises link and it cannot hold a trust of its own.
D is wrong: Cognito federates sign-in for web and mobile applications; it cannot domain-join Windows instances or provide integrated Windows authentication.
tldr: AWS Managed Microsoft AD plus a forest trust lets EC2 domain-join using existing on-premises AD accounts without duplicating them.

wrong_reasons.B: self-managed domain controllers mean patching, backups, monitoring and replication design, which is the ongoing administration the company wants to avoid.
wrong_reasons.C: AD Connector is a proxy that redirects requests to the on-premises directory rather than a directory in AWS, so every authentication depends on the on-premises link and it cannot hold a trust of its own.
wrong_reasons.D: Cognito federates sign-in for web and mobile applications; it cannot domain-join Windows instances or provide integrated Windows authentication.

question: A company stores critical design files in an Amazon S3 bucket. Last month an engineer deleted a prefix by mistake and the objects could not be recovered. The company wants deletions to be recoverable, wants permanently removing a version to require a second factor, and wants to keep storage cost in check. Which combination of actions should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)
hint: One setting keeps the previous copies, another makes permanent removal require a second factor, and a lifecycle rule stops the copies piling up.

options.A: Enable S3 Versioning on the bucket and add a lifecycle rule that expires noncurrent versions after 90 days.
options.B: Enable MFA Delete on the bucket, so that permanently deleting a version or suspending versioning requires an MFA code.
options.C: Enable S3 Object Lock in compliance mode with a 10-year retention period on every object.
options.D: Enable S3 Cross-Region Replication to a bucket in a second Region.
options.E: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket.

explanation: A is correct: with versioning on, a delete only writes a delete marker and the previous version can be restored, while a lifecycle rule that expires noncurrent versions after 90 days stops those older copies accumulating forever.

B is correct: MFA Delete requires an MFA code from the bucket owner's root credentials before a specific version can be permanently deleted or versioning suspended, which is the second factor the company asked for.
C is wrong: compliance mode would block every deletion for 10 years, including intentional cleanup, and force the company to store data it no longer needs.
D is wrong: replication copies objects to another Region for durability but does not by itself let you recover an object deleted by mistake, and it roughly doubles storage cost.
E is wrong: Transfer Acceleration speeds up long-distance transfers and has nothing to do with recovering deleted objects.
tldr: S3 Versioning (with lifecycle expiry) makes deletes recoverable, and MFA Delete adds a second factor before a version can be destroyed.

wrong_reasons.C: compliance mode would block every deletion for 10 years, including intentional cleanup, and force the company to store data it no longer needs.
wrong_reasons.D: replication copies objects to another Region for durability but does not by itself let you recover an object deleted by mistake, and it roughly doubles storage cost.
wrong_reasons.E: Transfer Acceleration speeds up long-distance transfers and has nothing to do with recovering deleted objects.

question: An internal REST API built with Amazon API Gateway must be reachable only from applications inside the company's VPCs and from its data center over AWS Direct Connect. It must not be reachable from the public internet, even by a caller with valid credentials. Which solution meets these requirements?
hint: Which API Gateway endpoint type has no public DNS at all, and which condition key pins it to your own endpoints?
keywords: only from applications inside the company's VPCs
must not be reachable from the public internet

options.A: Create the API as a private REST API, expose it through an interface VPC endpoint for API Gateway, and attach a resource policy that allows only requests arriving through that endpoint (aws:SourceVpce).
options.B: Keep a regional API and attach a resource policy that denies requests from source IP addresses outside the corporate range.
options.C: Keep a regional API and require IAM (SigV4) authentication on every method.
options.D: Create a VPC link so that the API integrates with private resources in the VPC.

explanation: A is correct: a private API has no public endpoint at all and can be called only through interface VPC endpoints, which the data center can reach over Direct Connect, and a resource policy keyed on the endpoint ID limits it to the approved VPCs.
B is wrong: a regional API keeps a public endpoint that anyone on the internet can reach and attempt to attack, even if a policy rejects most callers.
C is wrong: authentication controls who may call the API, but the endpoint itself is still publicly reachable, which the requirement forbids.
D is wrong: a VPC link governs how API Gateway reaches private backends; it does nothing about who can reach the API's own endpoint.
tldr: A private API Gateway endpoint plus a VPC-endpoint-scoped resource policy keeps an API reachable only from approved VPCs, never the internet.

wrong_reasons.B: a regional API keeps a public endpoint that anyone on the internet can reach and attempt to attack, even if a policy rejects most callers.
wrong_reasons.C: authentication controls who may call the API, but the endpoint itself is still publicly reachable, which the requirement forbids.
wrong_reasons.D: a VPC link governs how API Gateway reaches private backends; it does nothing about who can reach the API's own endpoint.

question: Amazon EC2 instances in a private subnet are configured with IPv6 addresses only. They must download software updates from IPv6 endpoints on the internet, but nothing on the internet may initiate a connection to them. Which solution meets these requirements?
hint: IPv6 addresses are globally routable. Which gateway is the IPv6 counterpart of a NAT gateway?
keywords: nothing on the internet may initiate a connection

options.A: Add an egress-only internet gateway to the VPC and route the subnet's ::/0 traffic to it.
options.B: Add a NAT gateway in a public subnet and route the subnet's ::/0 traffic to it.
options.C: Attach an internet gateway and route ::/0 to it, relying on security groups to block inbound connections.
options.D: Launch a NAT instance with an IPv6 address in a public subnet and route ::/0 to it.

explanation: A is correct: an egress-only internet gateway is the IPv6 equivalent of a NAT gateway for outbound-only traffic, because it is stateful, lets instances start outbound IPv6 connections, and refuses connections initiated from the internet.
B is wrong: a NAT gateway handles IPv4 translation, and although it can provide NAT64 so IPv6 hosts reach IPv4-only services, it is not the outbound path for IPv6 traffic to IPv6 destinations.

C is wrong: IPv6 addresses are publicly routable, so an internet gateway makes the instances reachable from the internet and the design depends entirely on every security group and network ACL staying correct.
D is wrong: a NAT instance is a self-managed IPv4 device and adds an instance to patch and scale.
tldr: An egress-only internet gateway is the IPv6 equivalent of a NAT gateway: outbound-only, nothing can initiate inbound.

wrong_reasons.B: a NAT gateway handles IPv4 translation, and although it can provide NAT64 so IPv6 hosts reach IPv4-only services, it is not the outbound path for IPv6 traffic to IPv6 destinations.
wrong_reasons.C: IPv6 addresses are publicly routable, so an internet gateway makes the instances reachable from the internet and the design depends entirely on every security group and network ACL staying correct.
wrong_reasons.D: a NAT instance is a self-managed IPv4 device and adds an instance to patch and scale.

question: A company must patch several hundred Amazon EC2 instances running Amazon Linux and Windows across three accounts on a monthly schedule, apply patches only inside an approved maintenance window, and produce a report showing which instances are missing patches. The company wants to avoid building its own tooling. What should a solutions architect recommend?
hint: One Systems Manager capability owns patch baselines, scheduling and compliance reporting.
keywords: report showing which instances are missing patches

options.A: Use AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager with patch baselines and patch groups, run it from a Systems Manager maintenance window, and review its patch compliance reporting.
options.B: Write an AWS Lambda function that runs the operating system update commands through Systems Manager Run Command on a schedule and records results in Amazon DynamoDB.
options.C: Build a new AMI every month and replace all instances using an Auto Scaling instance refresh.
options.D: Enable Amazon Inspector and let it install missing patches automatically.

explanation: A is correct: Patch Manager defines which patches are approved for each operating system in a baseline, targets instances by patch group or tag, applies them only during a maintenance window, and reports per-instance patch compliance across accounts with nothing custom to build.
B is wrong: this rebuilds Patch Manager by hand, including scheduling, error handling and compliance reporting.
C is wrong: replacing instances from a fresh AMI is a sound pattern but requires an image pipeline, only covers instances managed by an Auto Scaling group, and produces no missing-patch report.
D is wrong: Inspector finds and reports vulnerabilities but does not install patches.
tldr: Systems Manager Patch Manager applies approved patches on schedule within maintenance windows and reports compliance across accounts.

wrong_reasons.B: this rebuilds Patch Manager by hand, including scheduling, error handling and compliance reporting.
wrong_reasons.C: replacing instances from a fresh AMI is a sound pattern but requires an image pipeline, only covers instances managed by an Auto Scaling group, and produces no missing-patch report.
wrong_reasons.D: Inspector finds and reports vulnerabilities but does not install patches.

question: A company is migrating a legacy order-processing application to AWS. Its components communicate through an on-premises message broker using JMS and the AMQP 1.0 protocol, and the team cannot change the application code before the migration deadline. The broker must stay available if an Availability Zone fails. Which solution requires the LEAST application change?
hint: Keep the protocol, drop the servers. Which AWS service speaks the broker protocols the application already uses?
keywords: available if an Availability Zone fails

options.A: Migrate the queues to Amazon MQ for ActiveMQ in an active/standby deployment across two Availability Zones and repoint the application at the broker endpoints.
options.B: Replace the broker with Amazon SQS queues and rewrite the messaging layer to use the SQS API.
options.C: Replace the broker with Amazon SNS topics and HTTPS subscriptions.
options.D: Run the existing broker software on a single Amazon EC2 instance in one Availability Zone.

explanation: A is correct: Amazon MQ is a managed broker that speaks industry-standard protocols including JMS, AMQP, MQTT and STOMP, so the application keeps its existing messaging code, and an active/standby deployment fails over automatically to a second Availability Zone.
B is wrong: SQS has its own API and does not support AMQP, so the messaging layer would have to be reworked, which the deadline rules out.
C is wrong: SNS is push-based publish/subscribe with no broker protocol support, so it changes the application's interaction model entirely.
D is wrong: a single self-managed broker fails with its Availability Zone and leaves the company patching and operating the broker.
tldr: Amazon MQ speaks JMS/AMQP/MQTT/STOMP natively, so a legacy broker migrates without changing application code.

wrong_reasons.B: SQS has its own API and does not support AMQP, so the messaging layer would have to be reworked, which the deadline rules out.
wrong_reasons.C: SNS is push-based publish/subscribe with no broker protocol support, so it changes the application's interaction model entirely.
wrong_reasons.D: a single self-managed broker fails with its Availability Zone and leaves the company patching and operating the broker.

question: A regulator requires that a company keep a copy of certain Amazon S3 objects in a second AWS Region, that the copy exist within 15 minutes of the object being written, and that the company be able to demonstrate it met that window. Objects already in the bucket are in scope as well as new ones. What should a solutions architect do?
hint: Replication on its own promises no time limit. Which option adds one, and what covers the objects already in the bucket?

options.A: Enable S3 Cross-Region Replication with S3 Replication Time Control, turn on replication metrics and events, and run S3 Batch Replication for the existing objects.
options.B: Enable S3 Cross-Region Replication without Replication Time Control and rely on its best-effort replication.
options.C: Schedule an AWS DataSync task between the two buckets every 15 minutes.
options.D: Enable S3 Same-Region Replication and copy the destination bucket to another Region nightly.

explanation: A is correct: Replication Time Control commits to replicating 99.99% of new objects within 15 minutes and is backed by a service level agreement, replication metrics and events provide the evidence, and Batch Replication copies the objects that existed before replication was turned on.
B is wrong: standard replication is best effort with no time commitment and no metrics that prove the window was met.
C is wrong: a task that starts every 15 minutes leaves an object written just after a run waiting far longer than 15 minutes.
D is wrong: Same-Region Replication keeps the copy in the same Region, and a nightly copy is far outside the required window.
tldr: S3 Replication Time Control SLA-guarantees 15-minute cross-Region replication, with Batch Replication covering pre-existing objects.

wrong_reasons.B: standard replication is best effort with no time commitment and no metrics that prove the window was met.
wrong_reasons.C: a task that starts every 15 minutes leaves an object written just after a run waiting far longer than 15 minutes.
wrong_reasons.D: Same-Region Replication keeps the copy in the same Region, and a nightly copy is far outside the required window.

question: A company has connected its data center to a VPC with AWS Direct Connect. Applications in the VPC must resolve names in the on-premises domain corp.internal, and on-premises servers must resolve records held in an Amazon Route 53 private hosted zone that is associated with the VPC. Which combination of actions should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)
hint: DNS has to flow in two directions here, and Route 53 Resolver has a different endpoint type for each.
keywords: resolve names in the on-premises domain

options.A: Create a Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoint in the VPC with a forwarding rule that sends queries for corp.internal to the on-premises DNS servers.
options.B: Create a Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint in the VPC and point the on-premises DNS servers at its IP addresses for the private hosted zone's domain.
options.C: Associate the private hosted zone with the data center by adding the data center's CIDR range to the hosted zone.
options.D: Enable DNS hostnames on the VPC and have on-premises servers query the Amazon-provided DNS server at the VPC's base address plus two.
options.E: Create a second private hosted zone for corp.internal in Route 53 and copy the on-premises records into it by hand.

explanation: A is correct: an outbound endpoint with a forwarding rule sends queries that match corp.internal from the VPC to the company's own DNS servers, so applications in the VPC resolve on-premises names.
B is correct: an inbound endpoint provides Resolver IP addresses inside the VPC that on-premises resolvers can forward to, which is how the data center resolves private hosted zone records.
